It’s tough to escape the treadmill when the weather starts to turn. And while cruising through an easy run with entertainment is one thing, locking into intense speed intervals while staring at the same console is another. Without fresh scenery or a crew of training partners to pull you along, speedwork on the belt can test your focus before it tests your fitness.
Even professional runners know the feeling. When weather or logistics reroute a key workout indoors, they adapt and find ways to make the session productive, fast, and even fun.
Here, eight pros share the treadmill workouts they rely on to turn indoor interval sessions into serious gains.
1. Tempo Run With Incline Play
Pro runner: Joe Klecker, 2020 Olympian in the 10,000 meters, who made his marathon debut at the 2025 New York City Marathon and went on to earn a PR at the 2026 Boston Marathon, finishing in 2:05:56 for 13th place.
Joe Klecker got this workout from his mother, Janis Klecker, a fellow Olympian who competed in the marathon in the 1992 Barcelona Games.
“My mom used to do this workout when she was training for the marathon in Minnesota,” Klecker tells Runner’s World. “The nice thing was, if I finished, say six miles, then the next time I did it, I’d move the pace faster, but if I was only able to get maybe five miles in, then I would know the next time I need to keep the pace there until I was in good enough shape to do the full six miles.”
As for how to lock into the right effort: “I keep this one at marathon pace or somewhere between marathon and half-marathon pace because the incline makes it quite a bit harder,” Klecker says. “But this workout is fun because you could compare it over time throughout the winter to where you were, say, from December to February.”
How to do it:
- 2 mile easy warmup
- 4-6 miles at marathon or half marathon pace, alternating the incline between 0% and 4% every 0.25 miles for the duration
- 2 mile easy cooldown
2. Descending Fartlek
Pro runner: Amanda Vestri, who recently finished 15th among pro women at the 2026 Boston Marathon, recording a 2:24:49.
Amanda Vestri’s build for her 26.2 debut at the 2025 New York City Marathon, where she ran a 2:25:40, included a decent amount of treadmill training with workouts created by her former coach, Pete Rea of the now-defunct ZAP Endurance Group, which was based in Blowing Rock, North Carolina. The course is notoriously challenging and hilly, which was hard to closely simulate outside in North Carolina.
“If you live near flatter terrain, or you don’t have those rolling hills, treadmill workouts can be hugely beneficial for a race like New York,” Vestri tells Runner’s World. “I think it definitely prepared me for it.”
For her favorite workout, Vestri alternates inclines and declines, while pushing the pace. “With this workout, you’re starting with a longer interval, and then in between, you’re not jogging but rather floating and running at a steady rhythm about 40 to 50 seconds slower, and you end up getting a good amount of mileage in,” Vestri says.
How to do it:
- 3-mile easy warmup with 6 to 8 strides toward the end
- 8 minutes at marathon pace, alternating between 2.5% incline and -1.5% decline every 45 seconds

Google's (GOOG) investors have a few things in their favor coming into earnings day this week that Meta (META) investors weren't afforded when the tech giant reported a few negative surprises.
"Google has already done some of its fundraising and indicated a 'significant' increase in capex next year when it reported Q2, so that particular reckoning may be behind it," D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria wrote in a note on Monday. "It is worth noting that Mr. Brin and Mr. Page moved out of California before the 1/1/26 cutoff and may be able to avoid having to sell their shares. Which means that investors will be able to focus on the Anthropic-driven growth in Google Cloud."
Meta surprised investors last week on several fronts.
The company posted negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012 amid aggressive AI spending. It signaled more aggressive spending in coming quarters.
To fund that spending, it further surprised investors by establishing a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock, which effectively serves as a 2-for-1 stock split.
Under the scheme — in part designed to keep founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg working in California as the 5% billionaire's tax looms — existing shareholders will receive one new nonvoting Class C share for every Class A or Class B share they hold. Trading is slated to begin in January 2027.
Issuing nonvoting stock allows Zuckerberg to raise external capital for Meta's AI build-out without diluting his personal voting control over the tech giant.
Meta shares have come under pressure on fears Zuckerberg may have to sell shares to pay for his Prop 40 tax bill.

But as Luria pointed out, Google investors need not worry on this front.
Co-founder Larry Page bought two Miami estates for a combined $173.4 million, the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year. His co-founder, Sergey Brin, moved to the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe and also bought a home in Miami this year, Fortune reported.

This is the first cloud recovery method IBM has validated for interoperability with Terraform Self-Managed, self-hosted platform for defining and managing cloud infrastructure as code. Cloud rebuild is part of Cohesity Data Cloud Enterprise Edition.

JPMorgan Chase's (JPM +0.74%) asset management division recently released the 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report, an annual research report that includes 10- to 15-year return projections. For the first time, it has a returns forecast for Bitcoin (BTC +0.32%), and expects the top cryptocurrency to outperform the major asset classes.
It's another sign of the growing acceptance of cryptocurrency. CEO Jamie Dimon previously called Bitcoin a fraud, and as recently as 2025, he said he didn't see its value. However, a positive forecast doesn't necessarily mean Bitcoin is a slam-dunk investment.
What JPMorgan projected
JPMorgan's base case for Bitcoin is 10% annualized returns over the next 10 to 15 years, but the bank sees a wide range of potential returns. Its bear case is -11.2%, and its bull case is about 16.5%.
For perspective, JPMorgan forecasts annualized returns of 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 7.7% for small-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 5.6% to 6.6% for U.S. bonds. Real estate investment trusts (REITs) came in at 8.2%.
If JPMorgan's base cases are accurate, $100 invested in Bitcoin would grow to $259 over the next 10 years. The same amount invested in large caps would grow to $206.
This isn't a buy recommendation from JPMorgan
The press release for JPMorgan's report specifically noted that Bitcoin isn't included as an allocation. The bank also hasn't yet included Bitcoin in its main covariance matrices, the models it uses to determine how much of an asset belongs in a portfolio.
JPMorgan laid out two obstacles to Bitcoin portfolio use: volatility and unstable correlations with other assets. Cryptocurrency is known for its volatility, and in Bitcoin's case, JPMorgan assumes 55% annualized volatility, compared to 18% for U.S. large caps and 17.2% for gold.

Bitcoin's unstable correlations with other assets make it difficult to allocate in a portfolio. You can't count on it as a hedge or to balance out risk, because even though it's sometimes called "digital gold," Bitcoin doesn't perform that way. Gold has held its value during several stock sell-offs, whereas Bitcoin frequently falls with the stock market.
Is Bitcoin a screaming buy?
A small position in Bitcoin is worth considering if you have a high tolerance for risk and volatility. The cryptocurrency has historically outperformed stocks by a wide margin during its bull markets, with the trade-off that it suffers much greater losses during bear markets. Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (GOOGL -1.06%) reports third-quarter results on Wednesday, Oct. 28, and most of the attention will focus on the usual places. This includes how fast Google Cloud grew, whether Search held up, and what the capital spending number looks like. But one line matters more than any of them right now, and it sits a few pages deeper in the release: operating cash flow.
In the second quarter, Alphabet spent $44.9 billion on property and equipment and generated $39.1 billion in cash from operations. For the first time in recent memory, the company's free cash flow was negative, at $5.9 billion. : https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000066/googexhibit991q22026.htm That is not a rounding error for a business that generated $24 billion in free cash flow just two quarters earlier. Alphabet covered the gap by raising $49.6 billion in stock and $20.3 billion in debt in June. A company that spent a decade buying back shares has started selling them.
GOOG Alphabet
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/26/26
Google Cloud is doing its part
The bull case is that this is temporary, and the second-quarter earnings report gave that case real support. Google Cloud revenue grew 82% to $24.8 billion, and more importantly, cloud operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion from $2.8 billion a year earlier. That means cloud is now earning roughly $0.36 in operating profit per dollar of revenue, up from about $0.21. Consolidated operating margin expanded two points to 34%.
That is the chain investors need to see hold: cloud growth becomes cloud margin, cloud margin becomes operating income, and operating income becomes cash. In the second quarter, the first two links worked. The third did not.
Operating cash flow actually fell from $45.8 billion in the first quarter to $39.1 billion, even as operating income rose. Part of that was a nearly $7 billion build in inventory, notable for a company that now sells Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) chip systems through its cloud segment, as well as a jump in receivables. Those figures could reverse. But until they do, Alphabet is funding its artificial intelligence build-out with Wall Street's money, not its own.
What Alphabet needs to show
Management raised full-year capital expenditure guidance to $195 billion to $205 billion on the second-quarter call, up from $180 billion to $190 billion, according to Bloomberg Law. Alphabet generated $185.7 billion in operating cash flow over the trailing 12 months. Read those two numbers together, and the problem is obvious: At the current pace, the company is spending more than it makes, and the equity raise bought it time rather than a solution.
On Oct. 28, the metric to focus on is operating cash flow, and the question is whether it moves back toward the $45 billion to $50 billion range the company produced in late 2025 and early 2026. If it does, the working-capital drag was a blip, the cloud profits are real cash, and the capex budget is self-funding. The stock can keep working. If operating cash flow remains flat or slips again while capex climbs, Alphabet's AI story will be financed by shareholders, and the market will start pricing it that way.

The US Federal Trade Commission and 20 states sued Dollar General Corp. on Monday, alleging the discount retailer routinely charged customers more than the prices displayed on shelves or in advertisements.
Dollar General, which operates more than 21,000 stores, overcharged by millions of dollars in violation of federal and state consumer protection laws, according to a lawsuit filed in Tennessee federal court. The pricing discrepancies from 2019 through March 2026 led to almost 30,000 consumer complaints to the company, demonstrating “pervasive and systemic pricing inaccuracies,” federal and state enforcers said.
“Rather than ensuring its prices at checkout are accurate, for years Dollar General avoided implementing safeguards to prevent continued overcharging, effectively shifting the burden of its own operational shortcomings onto the very communities and consumers who can least afford it,” the complaint alleged.
Dollar General didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Between 2019 and 2026, the company entered into seven settlements in six different states related to inaccurate pricing, paying a total of $6 million in penalties, the complaint said.

The company, which publicly filed for an initial public offering on Monday, said it’s aware its efforts to secure power may face regulatory hurdles if there’s a perception its activities are impacting utility costs or the environment more broadly.

Before Florida lawmakers in 2022 enacted sweeping insurance law changes that cut the legs out of what had been called an excessive and burgeoning number of property claims lawsuits, they tinkered for years with ways to rein in the costly litigation.
One of the statutes, approved in 2021, required policyholders to give insurers 10 days’ notice before filing lawsuits. That law, the result of Senate Bill 76, was seen as a way to give carriers a second chance to settle a claim before litigation erupted.
But since then, questions have remained over whether the law applied to insurance policies written before the July 1, 2021 effective date of the statute, or only to claims or lawsuits filed after that date. Five Florida appeals courts have offered opinions on the retroactivity of Statute 627.70152, most of them differing in one way or another.
In 2023, the state’s 6th District Court of Appeal sided with the homeowner in a case known as Universal Property & Casualty Insurance vs. Rebecca Hughes. The judges found that the 2021 law did not apply retroactively and that the homeowner was not required to give pre-suit notice—even though Hughes’ suit was filed a month after the law took effect.
The 6th District’s opinion conflicted directly with the 4th District Court of Appeals, which had held in 2023 that the presuit notice requirement applies retroactively—to policies in effect at the time the law took effect. The 6th District asked the Supreme Court to settle the matter.
The justices answered on Oct. 22, upholding the 6th DCA and disapproving the 4th District’s ruling. The Florida Legislature had included no language in Senate Bill 76 that required retroactivity, the high court said. The policy period was from 2019 to 2020.
“So, on its face, no provision of section 627.70152 speaks to application of the statute to insurance policies issued before the statute’s effective date. And nothing in our precedent demands that we disturb that silence,” the opinion reads. “The correct answer is to respect the Legislature’s choice not to clearly require retroactive application of the statute.”
The lead plaintiffs’ attorney in the appeal, Matthew Danahy, of Tampa, said the Supreme Court ruling settles the conflict between the lower appellate courts’ 2023 opinions, strongly in favor of policyholders.
“The insurance industry pushed the retroactive application argument to try to further limit their insureds’ access to court, despite the fact that their policies were issued before the effective date of the statute and the absence of express language in the statute indicating that it was retroactive,” Danahy said in an email.
Another plaintiffs’ attorney who represents insureds lamented the fact that it took years to resolve the question.

Police in California are investigating the theft of trading cards worth at least $963,000 that were taken from a FedEx truck parked outside of a company that verifies memorabilia.
The truck was broken into on Oct. 13 near Professional Sports Authenticator, also known as PSA, which authenticates trading cards, autographs, comic books, and other memorabilia and grades their condition, Santa Ana Police Department spokesperson Natalie Garcia said in a news release. Pokémon and sports cards were among the items that were stolen, the release said.
The driver had left the truck unattended, Garcia said in a follow-up email Tuesday. How long the driver was gone is part of the investigation, she said.
The truck’s lock was gone and two pallets were taken, she said. A third pallet was disturbed.
“The estimated value of the stolen cards at the time of the incident was $963,000. However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined,” Garcia said in the news release.
Nick Andrews, a card collector near Boston, told The Associated Press the value of what was taken could be much higher.
PSA’s parent company, Collectors, said it has “deactivated the certificates for the stolen cards and notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items.”
The company also said it contacted affected customers directly and arranged for compensation based on fair market value.
Both FedEx and Collectors said they are working with law enforcement.
“The security of our customers’ shipments is a top priority,” FedEx spokesperson David Westrick said in a statement.
FedEx referred additional questions to police.
Some people who identified themselves as customers posted online that they got an email from PSA explaining what happened to their cards. They were worried they would never see them again or receive proper compensation.
Andrews, who collects vintage sports and Pokémon cards, told the AP in a phone interview that he was not affected by the theft but has heard from at least two dozen people who were.
“Thousands of cards, most likely, and millions of dollars, most likely,” he said of the losses collectors suffered.
He said one person who submitted cards for grading on behalf of several people told him that they lost half a million dollars in declared value.
PSA’s parent company did not get into specifics on losses in its statement.
“We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset,” the statement from Collectors said. “Our team is focused on supporting them. We take this incident seriously, and we will continue working with law enforcement to hold those responsible accountable.”

Utah’s lower legal blood alcohol concentration limit for drivers was associated with reduction in alcohol-related crashes over four years, according to a new study from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.
For the four years after the state lowered the limit to 0.05% Utah saw a nearly 9% reduction in alcohol-related crashes, according to an IIHS study.
Utah became the first state to lower its BAC threshold for impaired driving from 0.08% to 0.05% in 2018. It remains the only state with the lower limit.
IIHS researchers analyzed crash data from the first four years after the change and compared Utah’s alcohol-involved crash rates with those in Arizona, Colorado and Idaho.

The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off.
“The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.”
The Archiocese of New York covers the city’s boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics.

The Organ Transplant Service teams at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center started using robotic surgery for kidney transplants in 2018. Nationwide, more than 109,000 people are on waiting lists for organ procurement. (Photo courtesy of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center)
Federal regulators are cracking down on the nonprofits responsible for coordinating organ donations, aiming to begin shutting down substandard groups by early next year.
New criteria will score the organizations on donation and transplantation rates and will decertify the bottom tier, meaning their contracts with the federal government will be revoked. Many professional medical groups welcome more stringent evaluations. But the nonprofits strongly oppose aspects of the criteria and have filed lawsuits, warning of potential disruptions in some states or regions.
More than 109,000 people are on waiting lists nationwide for organ procurement, according to federal data as of July. The majority of patients await kidneys. Each day on average, about a dozen patients die waiting for an organ.
State- and region-based nonprofits known as organ procurement organizations recover organs from deceased donors and work with families and transplant centers to coordinate donations. The procurement organizations have faced heavy scrutiny in recent years, with media reports and research papers highlighting issues such as skipping over some transplant centers and sicker patients, which worsens racial and socioeconomic disparities in organ transplants.
The feds have shut down at least two groups in the past two years, citing questionable practices and saying that there were cases in which workers ignored signs of consciousness in donors.
Changes have been in the works for years. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services first announced the new evaluation framework in 2020, in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump. Earlier this year, CMS released proposed revisions to that rule.
Aiming for better accountability, transparency and oversight of the groups, as well as increasing patient protections and organ recovery, CMS will score the nation’s 55 organ procurement organizations based on their donation and transplantation rates.
It will rank them into three tiers: Top tier organizations — those calculated in the top 25% of organizations for donation and transplantation rates — would be automatically renewed for another four years. Those that fall in the second tier will have the opportunity to improve and reapply for certification, while those ranking in the bottom tier would be decertified entirely. Other nonprofits will then make bids to the federal government to take over their service areas, according to CMS.
The new evaluation method has stirred debate. Some medical and policy experts say better oversight of the nonprofits is long overdue, while organ procurement organizations say they will face logistical hurdles in coordinating lifesaving organs if some are shut down.
CMS hasn’t yet released which organization’s contracts will be renewed or dropped, but said in March that the process would begin sometime late this year. The current four-year contracts expire in January, but CMS has said it will issue extensions as needed to ensure organ transplants continue.
CMS did not provide a specific date in response to Stateline’s request for information about when it would release certification

Want to end redistricting wars? Start by uncapping the US House.
The U.S. Capitol on April 9 (Ashley Murray/States Newsroom).
Missouri’s congressional redistricting battle has taken voters on a dizzying tour of the court system leading up to the midterms. After trips to the Missouri Supreme Court and federal district court resulted in different rulings, the state took not one but two trips to the U.S. Supreme Court, which held – twice – that the state should use its 2022 congressional map for the November 2026 election. Voters will decide the fate of the new map through Proposition A.
The legal question that dominated these disputes was about whether Missouri could use a newly drawn map despite a valid referendum petition. But the process invokes a larger and more important question about our representation: why has control of a single congressional seat become so consequential that politicians are willing to fight over it in multiple court rooms instead of trusting voters to decide?
One way voters can take matters into their own hands is to support uncapping the U.S. House of Representatives. From our nation’s founding until the passage of the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, the House grew alongside the national population. The cap at 435 members created an artificial scarcityaround representation, and that scarcity is one of the drivers fueling the current gerrymandering wars, in Missouri and beyond.
With the same number of House seats representing a population that has more than tripled since 1929, each individual district has become larger, and political control of each one has become more consequential.
Missouri’s congressional delegation provides a particularly striking example. When the House was capped in 1929, Missouri had 16 seats in the House, representing a population of 3.6 million residents, or approximately 225,000 constituents per representative. By contrast, today Missouri has only eight House seats, representing a population of nearly 6.3 million, meaning that each representative has approximately 783,000 constituents. In other words, Missouri’s population has nearly doubled yet its House delegation has been cut in half.
The average Missourian now experiences a much lower quality of representation as a result, because even the most conscientious representatives struggle to serve such large districts. For example, Missouri’s 6thCongressional District, spanning all of northern Missouri from the Kansas border to the Mississippi River, includes 39 counties and is so large that it covers more square miles than nine U.S. states.
To be clear, uncapping the House is not a panacea for partisan gerrymandering. The process will always be political, and the parties will always compete to control the process. But expanding the House would reduce the artificial scarcity problem that has made each individual seat such an extraordinarily valuable political asset. More representation is also consistent with what the Founders intended – in Federalist No. 55, Madison warned against making the House too small, arguing that it must be large enough to secure “a full knowledge of the interest of its constituents,” and ensure “that its members are not lifted too far aloft from the mass of the citizens.”
Smaller districts would also mean more opportunities for voters to elect someone responsive to their communities and less political power concentrated in each individual seat.

Estate planning is just one of the topics I cover in Unspeakable, but as I've traveled to give talks and answer questions about the book, it's one that's coming up most frequently.

With a beat this small, the more telling changes sit further down the report.
So where did IBM’s quarter actually turn?
IBM’s Software Business Sped Back Up
The turn came in software, which generated 44.4% of IBM’s revenue in fiscal 2025, more than any other segment. Management said software revenue growth jumped four points from the second quarter to reach 9%. It also said the division led a broader pickup across IBM’s segments, with infrastructure growth rising to 5%.
Management said the biggest difference came from a single part of the software business. On the October 21 call, executives explained that transactional sales, the software IBM sells in individual deals rather than as recurring revenue, make up about 20% of the software book. These sales fell by double digits in the second quarter, taking 4 to 5 points off software growth. In the third quarter, they rose by double digits. This swing was larger than software’s four-point pickup. Management also said its automation business faced a tougher comparison.
How Much Of IBM’s Software Jump Was Catch-Up?
Management said about a quarter of the jump came from large deals that slipped out of the second quarter and closed in the third. The other three-quarters was new business. For transaction processing, its mainframe software, management said the deferred second-quarter deals landed on top of a normal third-quarter mainframe buying cycle.
For IBM as a whole, the quarter looks more like a recovery from the second quarter than a step up. Total reported revenue grew 4.7% from a year earlier, an improvement from 1.1% in the second quarter. That pace still trails the first quarter, when revenue grew 9.5%.

Management held its forecast for 2026 revenue growth at 4% to 5% at constant currency, the same range it gave in July. To gauge whether Adobe (ADBE) stock can jump 50%, look at a part of the company you may overlook: its faster-growing subscriptions for business professionals and consumers. In seven of the last ten calendar years, the stock rose 50% or more from one close to a later close in the same year. Yet the shares lost 27.0% over the past year, and you probably still think of Adobe as software for creative professionals. So how big are those subscriptions?
Business Professionals And Consumers Bring Adobe 29% Of Subscriptions
Adobe sold $1.91 billion of subscriptions to business professionals and consumers in fiscal Q3 2026, up 16% from a year earlier. That pace makes them the faster-growing group so far. Adobe’s subscriptions for creative and marketing professionals were far larger at $4.65 billion, but grew 13%.
Adobe maintains a wide reach with business professionals and consumers. On the September 10, 2026 call, management said monthly active users in this group rose more than 25% from a year earlier to over 900 million. The company is also targeting the next generation of business professionals by making student spaces in Acrobat available globally.
Adobe Is Choosing When To Turn Users Into Subscribers
Adobe says it will decide when to try to turn free users into paying subscribers. Management said on the September 10 call that the company is routing part of its traffic to its freemium products, which are free to start, to win customers and deepen their usage. Adobe will then convert those users into recurring revenue at the right time. This strategy, management added, balances winning new customers with growing recurring revenue.
Analysts questioned that approach on the call. When one analyst noted that net new annual recurring revenue was down 36% to 37% from a year earlier, management cited the shift toward freemium products as one of the drivers. Adobe finished fiscal Q3 2026 with $22.16 billion in remaining performance obligations, which represent contracted revenue the company has yet to book. That figure was up 8% from a year earlier.
Trading at 14.0 times Adobe’s last twelve months of earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500, the stock price appears to allow for little from those users. Adobe’s faster-growing business and consumer subscriptions show reported sales are still rising, but they do not settle the analysts’ questions about new recurring revenue. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue and earnings targets on the call, but it only reiterated its target of 10.2% growth in ending annual recurring revenue.
What Adobe Passed Up To Win New Users
Adobe opted not to focus on pricing actions in its creative business so it could keep adding users. Management said on the September 10 call that the company was glad it had held back. Pricing actions might have brought short-term relief, management said, but they mattered less than winning new users.
The creative business still makes up most of Adobe. For fiscal 2026, management targets $18.242 billion to $18.272 billion of subscription revenue from creative and marketing professionals, against $7.47 billion to $7.49 billion from business professionals and consumers. If more of Adobe’s new users do not start paying, the company will have skipped pricing actions in its largest business without the new subscribers to show for it.

Tropical Cyclone Arnab is expected to hit India’s east coast on Wednesday, marking a break in an otherwise calm season that’s been subdued by a severe El Niño.
Arnab is currently 859 kilometers (534 miles) southwest of Kolkata, packing top sustained winds of 213 kilometers per hour, according to the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center, equivalent to a Category 4 hurricane. The cyclone is forecast to intensify further before making landfall, though models are currently split on whether it will stall before or after crossing the coast, the center said.
El Niño has upended typical cyclone seasons around the world this year. The Atlantic Ocean is set for one of its lowest hurricane counts since 1941, while the Northwest Pacific Ocean is on track for one of its most intense typhoon seasons on record. Meanwhile, the North Indian Ocean has seen significantly below-average activity in recent months, with Arnab the first cyclonic storm.
“One of the key climatic events has been the suppression of the Indian monsoon and with it, the much reduced tropical cyclone activity, driven by the long reach of the El Niño,” said Christian Werner, managing director of Global Weather Climate Analytics.
Arnab is expected to bring moderate to intense rainfall across parts of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, and could cause widespread damage to standing crops and plantations including banana, papaya, and drumstick trees, according to the India Meteorological Department. Deluges over Nepal, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka are also possible, forecasts show.
The North Indian Ocean sees storm activity peak during two distinct periods of the year: before the monsoon, from April to June, and after the monsoon, from October to December.

The Justice Department for decades has deployed monitors across the country to watch the voting process. During President Joe Biden’s administration, the DOJ sent monitors to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections.
The 2026 monitoring program is larger, with the Justice Department announcing it will have a presence in all 50 states. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told States Newsroom on Monday that about 1,000 monitors will be involved but that the department won’t disclose the full list of monitored locations until Election Day — Nov. 3.
“Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day,” Pels said in a statement.
Lawsuits prompt unease
While election monitors, who watch polling places and election officials for compliance with federal voting rights laws, have long been a feature of U.S. elections, the Trump administration’s extraordinary moves to assert federal authority over state-run elections have left many Democrats and even some Republicans uneasy about this year’s expansive effort.
The Justice Department has sued dozens of states in an attempt to force election officials to turn over voter lists that contain sensitive personal data, such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. The DOJ has lost 27 cases so far, and won none.
Less than two weeks ago, the Justice Department sued California to block election officials from counting ballots from roughly 20,000 voters it says are suspected noncitizens.
And on Friday, the DOJ sued Alaska to preemptively prevent the certification of its U.S. Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses by less than the number of votes received by another candidate of the same name, citing the potential for voter confusion.
But concerns about DOJ monitors began building in August after Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, expressed reservations about monitors, calling their actions “very odd” after DOJ personnel watched voting in the state’s primary election.
Andrew Walchuk, senior policy director and counsel for voting & fair representation at the watchdog group Common Cause, told reporters last month that monitors in and of themselves are nothing new, pointing to the long history of the DOJ’s monitoring program.
“But with this administration, we will be watching their activity very closely,” Walchuk said.

Election experts have emphasized that even with a 1,000 monitors, the Justice Department presence across the country will be far too small to interfere with voting on a wide scale. The percentage of people without health insurance is growing
Dr. Navdeep Lehga sets up equipment in the exam room of a mobile clinic in Mendota, California in 2025. The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has grown in the past two years, according to a new report. (Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local)
The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has increased in the past two years, largely because many people can no longer afford Obamacare coverage after Congress allowed federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year.
The uninsured rate for adults ages 19-64 rose to 11.2% this year, up from 8.9% in 2024, according to a new analysis by the Commonwealth Fund, a health policy and philanthropic nonprofit.
Nearly half of the 7,362 working-age adults who participated in the group’s biennial health insurance survey said they were uninsured, underinsured, or experienced a gap in coverage this year. Half said they delayed or avoided getting medical care because of the cost, compared with 46% in 2022.
The subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes. But the aid was designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, and Congress allowed it to expire at the end of last year.
As a result, the percentage of working-age adults with health insurance from the marketplaces created under Obamacare, officially known as the Affordable Care Act, declined to 6% this year, from 8% in 2024.
The percentage of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid also declined, to 13% this year from 16% in 2022, as many states removed people from the rolls at the conclusion of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The increase in the uninsured rate almost certainly will accelerate in January, when the Republican tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act takes effect. That law will require many Medicaid recipients to prove they are working or engaging in approved community service activities for at least 80 hours a month.
The law also mandates that states verify enrollees’ Medicaid eligibility every six months.
Another factor in the growing percentage of people without coverage is the rising cost of healthcare, which is pushing up premiums for private insurance.
“It’s affecting people’s ability to pay off bills right away, and it’s having an effect on health plans,” said Sara Collins, a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund and the lead author of the report.
Almost a third of the survey respondents, whether insured and uninsured, said they currently had medical or dental bills or were paying off medical debt. And more than 70% of uninsured adults said they had cost-related problems getting care.
“I think it’s very concerning,” Collins said. “We know from our survey data that not going to get care isn’t and just generally is not good for people’s health over the long run.”
The rise in the uninsured rate comes after a long period of progress: Between 2010 and 2025, the overall uninsured rate in the United States fell by half, to 8% from nearly 16%, largely because of the Affordable Care Act.

The Western District Court of Appeals found that a man resentenced in 2023 must receive credit for time served on all four concurrent sentences
Deandre Pointer, serving four concurrent 23-year-sentences in the Missouri Department of Corrections, won a ruling Tuesday that he must get credit for all time he has served on all four counts of his conviction. If he had lost, Pointer would have been incarcerated for 40 years. He is shown in a 2025 interview (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
A Missouri man who should have been eligible for release in 2024 remains in prison because the state miscalculated his credit for time he had already served, the Missouri Western District Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday.
Deandre Pointer was sentenced to 23 years in the Department of Corrections on four counts, two of second-degree murder and two of armed criminal action, with the sentences to run concurrently. He received the sentence in 2023 after a Jackson County judge determined Pointer was abandoned by his public defender in a post-conviction case filed after his original sentence was handed down in 2005.
When the resentencing was finished, Pointer thought he would be out in about a year, when he had served the required 85% of the sentence. But when a Missouri Department of Corrections record clerk finished processing his paperwork, his projected release date was 2044.
The department misapplied the law on how to calculate his sentence, Judge Alok Ahuja wrote in the court’s unanimous opinion.
“The Missouri Supreme Court has held that, ‘in construing (state law), we are guided by the principle that criminal statutes must be ‘construed strictly against the (s)tate and liberally in favor of the defendant,’” Ahuja wrote.
The 2023 resentencing changed both the charge in one count, from first- to second-degree murder, and the way the sentences were imposed, from consecutive to concurrent.
“Pointer’s conviction and sentence for first-degree murder on Count 1 must be treated as if they never occurred,” Ahuja wrote.
In a 2025 interview with The Independent, Pointer said he pursued a new sentence because he was a victim of crime, forced to help the perpetrator out of fear for his own safety.
The stress of having to fight for release after winning his resentencing has taken a severe toll, he said at the time.

“I never took anxiety meds,” Pointer said. “Never in my life. Now, you know, I have to take anxiety meds just to have a functional day.”
Pointer’s attorney, Kent Gipson, said in an email that Pointer is pleased with the ruling but knows it will not result in his immediate release. The state can seek rehearing or transfer to the Missouri Supreme Court, and Gipson said he expects it to challenge the decision.
The Western District decision overturned a February ruling from Cole County Circuit Judge Brian Stumpe that found the department had calculated the sentence correctly.
“It should have never come to this,” Gipson said. “If the (corrections) officials had done this earlier, it would have likely resulted in my client receiving a parole hearing and an outdate three years ago.”

Mark Kiptoo has had some pretty memorable trips to Frankfurt. He won the city's marathon in 2014, returned four years later to set a then-world record for runners over 40, and on Sunday added another achievement to the list. This time, at 50 years old.
The Kenyan distance runner finished the Frankfurt Marathon on October 25 in 2:15:24, averaging roughly 5:10 per mile across 26.2 miles. He placed 13th overall, but his performance was particularly impressive for another reason: It was the fastest marathon ever recorded by a man in the 50–54 age group—and it wasn't especially close.
For 35 years, the M50 record belonged to South Africa's Titus Mamabolo, who ran 2:19:29 in Durban in July 1991. Kiptoo cut four minutes and five seconds off that mark on Sunday, a substantial improvement that now awaits official ratification by World Masters Athletics.
Kiptoo has barely had time to get used to being 50. He celebrated his birthday on June 21, less than two months after finishing 2:12:21 at the Geneva Marathon. That performance came too early to qualify for an M50 record, but it offered a pretty good preview of what he could do once he entered the age group.
Frankfurt wasn't even his first record-setting performance this month. On October 4, Kiptoo won the San Sebastián Half Marathon in Spain in 1:03:57, establishing a new M50 world-best time for the distance. Three weeks later, he was back on a starting line, this time with twice as many miles to cover.
Kiptoo didn't start competing until he was 28, entering his first race in 2004 while serving in the Kenyan Air Force. He went on to win the African 5,000-meter title in 2012, but didn't make his marathon debut until age 37. That first 26.2 was in Frankfurt, where he finished second in 2013, just one second behind the winner.
He also lost roughly a year of training to Achilles tendon trouble and the pandemic, according to the Frankfurt organizers. He returned to win the Zurich Marathon three years in a row from 2023 through 2025, clocking 2:09:16 in his last victory at age 48.
Before Sunday's race, Kiptoo told organizers he hoped his running would inspire people not to give up or stop taking care of their bodies as they got older. Running a 2:15 marathon at 50 certainly gives him a pretty persuasive example to point to.

Wells Fargo and Merrill Agree to Pay $4.4 Million Over Small Stock Trades. What Happens When Retirement Investors Pay Too Much to Trade?
State regulators just forced two major brokerages to pay back millions in commissions their customers never knew they were losing. The same quiet erosion could be happening inside your 401(k) right now.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Small stock trades aren’t always cheap ones. On Oct. 15, state securities regulators announced a $4.4 million settlement involving two Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC | WFC Price Prediction) brokerage units and Merrill Lynch, part of Bank of America (NYSE: BAC). The North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA) said the firms had charged unreasonable commissions on thousands of small-dollar stock trades.
What Regulators Found on 256,000 Small Trades
Massachusetts regulators led a multistate investigation that uncovered unreasonable commissions on more than 256,000 stock trades over five years. The problem was minimum commissions, which can turn even a modest transaction into an expensive one.
The two Wells Fargo units collected nearly $3.9 million in unreasonable commissions across approximately 228,243 trades between Sept. 30, 2020, and Oct. 1, 2025. Merrill Lynch accounted for another $549,000 in excessive charges during the same period.
Affected customers in participating states will receive refunds plus interest, and the firms must certify that they’ve changed their commission practices. The investigation concerned retail brokerage accounts, not specifically 401(k)s. But workplace retirement investors can face trading commissions through brokerage windows, along with fund expenses and other charges that quietly eat into their savings.
A $250,000 Balance and a Fee Nobody Noticed
Picture a hypothetical 55-year-old with $250,000 in his 401(k). He never sees a separate bill for investment expenses, so he assumes his plan costs him nothing. But his funds and plan charges run an extra 0.5 percentage point a year compared with similar, lower-cost options.
On his current balance, that difference amounts to roughly $1,250 in one year, assuming the balance doesn’t change.
Now stretch the comparison over a decade. Suppose the cheaper portfolio earns 6% annually after fees, while the more expensive one earns 5.5%. With no additional contributions, his $250,000 would grow to approximately $447,700 in the cheaper option, compared with $427,000 in the pricier one.
That’s a difference of nearly $20,700 from an additional half-percentage-point in annual costs, compounded over 10 years.
Four Places 401(k) Costs Hide
- Fund expense ratios. These expenses are built into the fund’s returns rather than billed separately on your statement. You can find them in your plan’s investment disclosures and fund documents, but it’s easy to overlook their effect on your balance.
- Administrative and recordkeeping fees. These pay for running the plan: recordkeeping, legal work and the website. Some plans charge a flat dollar amount and others take a percentage of assets. When they come out of your account, they show up on your statements.
- Managed account or advice fees. A 2025 NEPC survey found that 46% of participating retirement plan sponsors offered managed accounts. These services may charge an additional asset-based fee on top of the expenses of the underlying investments.

Cisco Is Up 47%, IBM Is Down 13%. Which Dividend Stock Is Better for Retirement?
Cisco and IBM have moved in opposite directions this year, and that gap reshapes which one actually puts more money in a retiree's pocket over time. The answer depends on which trade-off you can afford to make.
Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO | CSCO Price Prediction) or IBM (NYSE:IBM): which old-guard tech dividend holds up better for someone saving for retirement right now? This year, the two stocks have gone in opposite directions. Cisco is up 46.77% year to date at $111.03. IBM is down 13.13% at $252.18. That gap changes how much income a new buyer gets today.
We compared the two on three things that matter to anyone living off dividends: current income, payout safety and the balance sheet, and the business growth that pays for future raises.
Current Income: IBM Writes the Bigger Check
IBM yields 2.67%, compared with 1.56% for Cisco. Its forward annualized dividend is $6.76 per share. Cisco’s is $1.68. IBM has paid consecutive quarterly dividends every year since 1916, and its April 2026 raise was its 31st consecutive annual increase. Cisco’s run stands at 15 consecutive years.
IBM’s weak spot is how slowly the payout grows. Its quarterly dividend went from $1.66 in early 2024 to $1.69, a gain of about 1.8%. Over the same period, Cisco’s rose from $0.39 to $0.42, about 7.7%. Still, for retired people spending income now, IBM pays far more per dollar invested. Winner: IBM.
Payout Safety and Balance Sheet: Cisco Has More Cushion
Cisco paid $6.6 billion in dividends in fiscal 2026 out of $14.18 billion in operating cash flow, so the dividend used about 47% of operating cash. Its forward dividend works out to roughly 33% of the low end of fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance, which is $5.05 to $5.11. Cisco closed the fiscal year with $15.9 billion in cash and investments. It also has $8.1 billion left on its buyback authorization.
IBM’s coverage is tighter. Over nine months, it paid $4.8 billion in dividends against about $8 billion of free cash flow, or 60%. Its forward dividend is about 58% of trailing EPS of $11.72. Debt stood at $63.8 billion, including $12.7 billion tied to its financing arm, against $11.1 billion in cash. That follows $11.4 billion in acquisitions this year. CFO Jim Kavanaugh described “a solid investment-grade balance sheet,” and he’s right, but Cisco has more room for error. Winner: Cisco.
Business Momentum: Cisco’s AI Networking Cycle Pulls Ahead
Cisco’s fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 17.6% to $17.25 billion. Non-GAAP EPS of $1.22 beat the $1.17 estimate, its fifth straight beat. Product orders rose 35%, and AI infrastructure orders reached $9.3 billion for the year. Chief Executive Chuck Robbins said, “We believe we are only at the beginning of this super cycle.” The weak spot is gross margin, which fell to 66.3% from 68.4% as AI hardware made up more of sales.
IBM’s third-quarter revenue grew 4.7% to $17.10 billion, with Red Hat up 11%. Consulting grew just 0.2%, and IBM Z revenue fell 20%. Full-year guidance calls for 4% to 5% constant-currency growth. That rate supports small, steady raises and little more. Cisco’s valuation premium is modest: 20 times forward earnings versus 17 for IBM. Winner: Cisco.

In brief
- Intel, Oracle, IBM and IonQ joined the list of companies objecting to trading of their shares on OKXICE TSV, according to its Oct. 26 notice.
- The total has climbed from nine on Oct. 15 to 26, though the notices don’t explain the objections or their effect.
- The notice says it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in self-custodied wallets would be protected by SIPC if the tokenizer’s broker-dealer failed.
The tech sector’s resistance to tokenized stocks keeps building.
Intel, Oracle, IBM, and quantum computing firm IonQ are the latest companies to object to having their shares traded on OKXICE TSV, according to an updated public notice from the venue dated Monday.
The planned platform, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, now lists 26 objecting issuers.
That’s up from 22 in its Oct. 23 notice, which added Wells Fargo, Cisco, and Marvell. The tally stood at 16 on Oct. 19 and nine on Oct. 15, when the first batch included Verizon, Broadcom and UnitedHealth Group. In less than two weeks, the list has nearly tripled.
Technology companies dominate the roster. Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Arm, Cisco, and now Intel and Oracle have all objected, along with banks Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo.
IBM and IonQ add two quantum computing players. As before, the notices don’t explain the companies’ reasons or what an objection means for whether a stock can trade on the platform.
OKXICE TSV plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.
Users must pass identity and sanctions checks and hold a nontransferable “soulbound” token to trade. The venue is set to operate under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.
The latest notice highlights a key risk for investors. Each token represents a claim on a real share held by a third-party “tokenizer” through a registered broker-dealer. If that broker-dealer failed, the notice says, it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in a self-custodied wallet would count as customer property or be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which protects brokerage customers when firms fail.
The notice also says trades must be fully funded, with no margin or borrowing. Liquidity providers don’t have to be registered market makers and can pull their liquidity at any time.
OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before unveiling plans for the venue this month.

Banks that keep outside AI agents out of customer accounts are guarding their own revenue rather than their customers, Bianco Research president Jim Bianco said on Unchained’s Bits + Bips during a live stream on Oct. 26.
“Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?” he asked.
His example was JPMorgan Chase, which keeps third-party AI agents from signing in to Chase accounts or acting on them for customers. Jamie Dimon, the bank’s CEO, explained the policy to analysts on Oct. 13, warning of “rogue agents” and saying JPMorgan is “not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company” because that is “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.” A spokesperson told Fortune that “protecting our customers is our top priority,” adding, “We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers.”
Citi, Bank of America and Wells Fargo have taken steps to limit third-party agents as well, and Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster has said the brokerage is shutting out third-party agents that try to move funds in customer accounts. Wells Fargo’s revised online access agreement, which takes effect Nov. 24, says transactions by an AI agent a customer authorizes are treated as the customer’s own, and makes the customer responsible for the agent’s unintended actions until the customer tells the bank it has revoked the agent’s access.
Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.
A Model Built on Friction
Bianco said the traditional finance “business model is based on laziness.” Customers don’t want to log in every day to move idle cash into a money market fund, he said, but an agent could do it for them. In his account, banks profit by investing deposits that pay the customer nothing. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said.
He put the money sitting in “zero-yielding bank accounts” at $4 trillion. Noninterest-bearing deposits in the domestic offices of U.S. banks came to about $4.04 trillion at the end of June, roughly 21% of domestic deposits, according to the FDIC’s Quarterly Banking Profile. That category includes business operating accounts, not only household savings. JPMorgan Chase Bank held $628.8 billion of it, about 28% of its domestic deposits, according to FDIC BankFind data.
Bianco made the same case about credit cards, saying issuers want cardholders to pay annual fees without making full use of their points, while some users have turned to AI agents to maximize rewards.
Pushback From Customers
Bianco predicted that customers would press for access anyway, noting that people already trade away their privacy online. “I think the public is gonna start demanding more and more of this,” he said.
Co-host Ram Ahluwalia, founder and CEO of Lumida Wealth Management, agreed on the motive. “They’re protecting themselves,” he said on the stream, adding that “the agents here are acting as fiduciaries of the customer.” He cautioned against overstating the risk of agent-driven deposit flight, though, since frictions such as opening a new bank account remain.

Alphabet has spent years designing its own AI chips, known as tensor processing units, or TPUs. For most of that time, these chips mainly served Google's own products and its cloud customers. This year, though, Alphabet started selling TPU systems directly to customers who want to run them in their own data centers.
So, why might the TPU be Alphabet's quietest advantage? Let's find out.

Not long ago, some investors worried the company would be a casualty of the AI era, with the idea that chatbots would pull users away from Google Search -- if that happened, it would clearly hurt advertising, which is Alphabet's bread and butter. Those worries haven't played out. In the second quarter, Google Search revenue grew 17%, and Google advertising represented 68% of total revenue.

Where the TPU fits in
Here's where the chip comes in. Unlike a general-purpose chip, a TPU is designed with AI workloads in mind, and Alphabet has refined the technology across multiple generations. That gives the company two potential benefits. First, it can run its own AI services and those of its cloud customers on hardware it controls, rather than relying solely on Nvidia's supply and pricing. Customer satisfaction with total loss auto insurance claims fell for a third straight year, while satisfaction improved for claims involving repairable vehicles, a new study looking at this year shows.
Customer satisfaction with total loss claims fell 12 points on a 1,000-point scale in 2026, marking a 46-point decline since 2023, according to the JD Power 2026 U.S. Auto Claims Satisfaction Study.
However, satisfaction with claims involving repairable vehicles improved four points and overall auto claims customer satisfaction was unchanged from last year at 700.
Overall, 26% of auto insurance claims were classified as total losses this year, up from 16% four years ago. The growing share of total losses reflects rising vehicle repair costs, consumers keeping vehicles longer and higher deductibles removing smaller repairs from the claims process, according to the study. Affordability pressures also led some customers to drop rental coverage or increase deductibles, complicating the claims experience.
Repair cycle times have improved as claim volumes have declined and repair shops have more capacity. Average repair cycle times fell to 15.3 days in the first quarter of 2026, down 10 days from the first quarter of 2024, the study shows.
The study also found differences in customer satisfaction based on how effectively insurers communicate across channels. Satisfaction averaged 804 among customers who strongly agreed their insurers provided a seamless experience across communication channels, compared with 390 among customers who disagreed.
The study shows that insurers provided a seamless cross-channel experience 54% of the time, one of the lowest-performing measures in the study. Problems cited included unclear explanations, customers having to use multiple channels to get answers and digital tools that did not work as expected.
Amica ranked highest in overall customer satisfaction with a score of 775, followed by Nationwide at 743 and Automobile Club of Southern California (AAA) at 740.
The study examines auto claims experiences in order of importance: trust, fairness of settlement, people, time to settle claim, communication, ease of resolving claim, ease of starting claim and digital channels. These actions stand in contrast to the Trump administration’s sizable investments and outspoken advocacy for bolstering the coal industry more broadly, the researchers contend.

The Delaware Supreme Court has upheld a Chancery Court ruling ordering Verisk Analytics Inc. to keep working on a $2.35 billion acquisition of roofing software maker AccuLynx.
Verisk tried to pull out of the deal last December after the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notified it that it had not completed its review of the transaction by the termination date of December 26. AccuLynx went to court to force Verisk to complete the deal.
Verisk had announced its plan to acquire AccuLynx in July 2025 and initially said it expected to close by the third quarter of 2025. AccuLynx and Verisk believed that the merger presented only minimal antitrust risk, as the companies did not compete horizontally or have a vertical supplier-customer relationship.
After last week’s Delaware Supreme Court ruling, Verisk said that it would comply with the ruling but cannot guarantee that the merger will be finalized.
Acculynx objected to Verisk’s exit from their agreement, claiming Verisk was responsible for the FTC delay that it then tried to use to walk away from their merger agreement.
In August, Chancery Court Judge Bonnie David agreed with AccuLynx. The judge found that Verisk’s termination was invalid because Verisk’s own “willful conduct caused the failure of a condition to closing.”
Verisk had answered no when the FTC first asked whether Verisk had ever terminated integration discussions with an AccuLynx competitor or rejected a request for an enhanced integration. The FTC had information that Verisk had in fact done so with a company called ServiceTitan. So the FTC asked again and as a result of having to issue a second request told Verisk it could not meet a December 26 deadline for review. Days later, Verisk purported to terminate the merger agreement on the extended termination date.
Acculynx asked the court to order Verisk to honor the merger agreement, including by using reasonable efforts to obtain clearance by the FTC and to close the merger if the FTC approves the transaction. AccuLynx also asked for damages in the amount of $3.85 million, plus prejudgment interest.
The Chancery Court ruled that AccuLynx was entitled to the order of specific performance against Verisk. The court also approved the damages for AccuLynx, finding that Verisk had waived its right to oppose the damages.
The court noted that the parties specifically agreed in the merger agreement that a party could not terminate if its own “willful conduct” was the “primary cause” of the failure to satisfy a condition. “It is not inequitable to hold the parties to their bargain,” the judge stated.
Verisk objected to the performance order requiring it to pursue the deal, arguing in part that such a remedy was not available where damages would provide adequate relief.
However, the Chancery Court noted that in addition to any other rights and remedies, the merger agreement made it clear that AccuLynx as seller had the right to enforce the obligations of the buyer “not only by an action or actions for damages but also by an action or actions for specific performance, injunctive and/or other equitable relief.”
The judge directed the parties to submit a proposed form of final order to implement the ruling.

A lawsuit filed on Friday involving the pay practices of Chili’s operator Brinker International is seeking to strike down New York state’s lower minimum wage for workers who earn tips, which it claims fuels the sexual and racial harassment of workers.
The proposed class action in federal court in Brooklyn by three former Chili’s employees claims that New York’s policy, which most other US states share, allows Brinker to force employees to rely on tips and exposes them to unlawful discrimination.
“Brinker promotes a culture in which tipped service employees make customers ‘feel special,’ even at the expense of their dignity and safety,” the lawsuit says.
Brinker did not respond to a request for comment. The New York Attorney General’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the challenge to the state law.
Many worker advocates have for years called for the elimination of sub-minimum wages that companies may pay to workers who earn tips under federal and most state laws, as long as tips make up the difference.
In New York, where the minimum wage is $16 an hour or $17 in and around New York City, food service workers who earn tips may be paid $10.70 or $11.35 an hour. The federal tipped minimum wage is $2.13 an hour, compared with the traditional minimum wage of $7.25, and applies in states that do not set their own minimums.
RELYING ON TIPS
Advocates say that because tips are discretionary and unpredictable, they should supplement workers’ incomes rather than make up most of their pay. The lawsuit against Brinker says that relying on tips forces workers to tolerate conduct such as sexual harassment and customers’ potential racial bias.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said in the lawsuit that they plan to expand the case to include a nationwide class of Chili’s workers.
Brinker operates more than 1,200 Chili’s restaurants in the US, including 36 in New York. The company also owns Maggiano’s Little Italy, an Italian restaurant chain with about 50 US locations.
The lawsuit claims that Chili’s reliance on customer ratings to determine workers’ schedules, shifts and table assignments is also unlawful. The ratings system can be racially biased, the lawsuit says, and can make it difficult for servers to reject unwanted advances from customers for fear of a poor rating.
The named plaintiffs, three former employees at a Chili’s in the Glendale section of Queens in New York City, claim they were routinely subjected to sexual advances and inappropriate comments and that management did not adequately protect workers from harassment.

A Washington contractor was fined $48,803 after a roofer was killed when he fell through a skylight.
Leslie & Campbell Inc. of Union Gap was fined $48,803 after a roofer fell more than 25 feet through an unguarded skylight to the concrete floor of a fruit packing warehouse in Wapato, according to the Washington State Department of Labor & Industries.
L&I cited the company after investigators found it had not guarded the skylight, identified skylights as a fall hazard or adequately trained workers on the danger.
The company is appealing the citation and fine.
L&I also issued penalties against other roofing companies and subcontractors in recent months:
- Roof Doctor Inc. of Olympia received the largest fine, $238,680, on June 30 for four willful serious and two serious fall protection violations. A portion of a roof collapsed beneath a worker in Tumwater, and inspectors determined his safety rope was too long to arrest his fall. The worker was hospitalized. Roof Doctor and its associated companies have been cited for more than 80 safety violations since 2004, including 34 for failing to ensure workers wore fall protection, according to L&I. The business is appealing the latest citation.
- Dabella/Reve Exteriors LLC of Marysville was fined $176,580 on Aug. 19 for two willful serious violations involving failure to protect subcontractor employees from falls and ensure they wore required protective equipment. Some violations repeated findings from earlier inspections, according to L&I. The company is appealing. Its subcontractor on the same job, Suruka House LLC, was fined $34,668 for repeatedly failing to ensure workers wore fall protection and other required protective equipment.
- Bartlett Homes & Roofing LLC of Veradale was fined $179,964 on June 3 for willful serious and repeat serious violations. Inspectors found two workers were not connected to a fall protection system, anchors were improperly installed and one worker’s fall restraint rope had enough slack that it would not have prevented him from hitting the ground. The company is appealing. Ivan’s Roofing Spokane LLC, a subcontractor on the same job, was fined $37,415 for workers not using fall protection, unsafe ladder use and failure to ensure first aid was available to injured workers.
- Money collected from fines goes into the workers’ compensation supplemental pension fund, which is earmarked to help injured workers and families of workers who died on the job.
